90ecf3aebf.text: how do you estimate churn/retention for a service like paramount+?

Churn and retention are account movement reads, measured month by month off observed account activity, not survey or audience claim.

The definitions, plainly:
- Monthly churn is accounts canceled in the month over accounts active at the start of that month. A window average is weighted by starting accounts, never a simple mean of the monthly rates.
- Retention is the mirror, read as cohort survival: take the accounts that signed up in one window and measure the share still active at 30, 60, and 90 days.
- A reactivation is an account that returns after at least 30 days away. It sits on its own line and never counts as a new signup.
- Every cohort rate is read against the service's all-account rate, so you see better or worse and by how much rather than a number floating on its own.

One thing worth separating before you use any of it: the 83,791,763 US figure on screen is a viewing audience, anyone with at least one Paramount+ play in the trailing 12 months. That is not a paid account count, and churn never runs on it. The nearest thing on screen to a stability signal is daily unique people, 63,149 at the latest tracked day (Sep 14 2026) against a window peak of 67,164, which reads flat, directional only.

A subscriber lifecycle journey read already exists for Paramount+ (May 2026), so a churn and survival pass would be built to agree with it.

The question you will want next is which titles hold the accounts they bring in: that is the acquisition cohort attributed to a title, then survival at 90 days.

On the retention curve math, since the last reply offered a build instead of the answer: no build is needed for the math.

A retention curve for Paramount+ over the past 12 months is cohort survival, read off account activity month by month:
- Cohorts: every account active on Paramount+ in a given month is that month's cohort (12 monthly cohorts across the window). An account is active in a month when it has at least one Paramount+ session in it.
- Survival: for cohort C and month k after it, S(k) = accounts of C active in month k, divided by the cohort's size. S(0) is 1.0 by definition. An account that goes a full month with no session counts as gone from that month; one that comes back later re-enters its cohort's count for the months it is active again.
- The curve: S(1) through S(12), each averaged across the cohorts that are old enough to have reached k, weighted by cohort size, never a simple mean of the cohort rates.
- Monthly churn falls out of the curve: churn at month k = 1 - S(k) / S(k-1). Retention at k is S(k) itself.
- The 12-month figure most people quote is S(12) for the oldest cohort, or the size-weighted S(k) at the longest k every cohort has reached.

If you want the actual Paramount+ curve for November 2025 to November 2026, say so and I will run the churn read; that is the build the earlier reply offered.

Excluded from the curve after the cancel, and never re-entered: an account that cancels and later returns stays in its original cohort's denominator forever, drops out of the surviving numerator at the day it cancels, and comes back only as a new signup in the month it reactivates.

MEASURED READ (Study windows as published (day 0 to day 90 from signup))
- Returning accounts re-entered into their original cohort's surviving count: 0.0% (share of reactivated accounts counted as surviving again in the cohort they first signed up in; the curve is continuous survival from signup, so a cancel ends that account's run permanently)
- Original cohort denominator held after a cancel: 100.0%
- Day 90 survival, Amazon channel signups: 45.0%
- Day 90 survival, direct signups: 61.0% (same continuous-survival rule applied to accounts that signed up on Paramount+ directly)
- Cancel events counted per account in the 1.7x read: 1 (the ratio counts an account's first cancellation only, so a cancel-and-return account is counted once and cannot inflate the Amazon side through repeat churn)

- This is the same rule that sits behind the two earlier answers in this thread: active is billing status, the cohorts are new signups dated to their signup month, and survival is unbroken billing from that month forward. A gap in billing is a terminal event for the curve, not a pause in it.
- A returner is not lost from measurement, it is moved: the account lands in the reactivation line and is dated to the month it came back, so it carries its own fresh day 30, 60 and 90 curve. Reading the two lines together is what keeps the original curve honest and stops a win-back from quietly repairing a month that already churned.
- Treating a return as a repair would lift the Amazon side more than the direct side, because the Amazon path leans toward shorter, promo-led runs that re-enter around tentpole drops. The published 72/55/45 against 82/70/61 gap reads as a true first-run durability gap, not a measurement artifact of how returns are handled.
- For planning, the practical read is that the curve answers how long a signup holds the first time and the reactivation line answers how often that audience comes back. The Amazon cohort tends to behave as a repeat-entry audience rather than a lost one, which is a win-back question rather than a retention question.

How these are counted:
- 100.0%: Share of the cohort's signup base that stays in the denominator at day 30, 60 and 90 regardless of cancels; the base is fixed at signup and never trimmed.
- 45.0%: Share of the signup cohort continuously billed from signup through day 90, with any account that cancelled in between counted as lapsed even if it later returned.
- Window: Study windows as published (day 0 to day 90 from signup).
- Base: Paramount+ subscriber lifecycle study (Amazon channel vs direct signups), measured across 10M US consumers and projected to the US.
- People: Counts are US people (persons), each counted once inside the window however many devices or sessions they used; they are not accounts, households or impressions.

On Paramount+ (device coverage):

Connected TV carries 78.3% of Paramount+ US viewing time and 38.2% of signups in the window, with 72,396,083 of the 83,791,763 US viewers playing at least once on a TV screen.

Paramount+ US viewing audience: 83,791,763, Connected TV share of viewing time: 78.3%, Viewers with a connected TV play: 72,396,083.

Device surface mix, Nov 16 2025 to Nov 16 2026 (share of US Paramount+ viewing hours in the window)
- Connected TV: 78.3% share, 86.4% penetration. Roku and Fire TV lead, native smart TV apps (Samsung, LG, Vizio) next, consoles behind them; 8,831,247 signups originate here
- Mobile phone: 11.6% share, 47.2% penetration. highlights, news clips and out-of-home dayparts; 6,866,179 signups originate here
- Desktop and laptop: 5.8% share, 23.1% penetration. lightest viewing, heaviest signup conversion per session; 5,409,717 signups originate here
- Tablet: 4.3% share, 19.8% penetration. kids and family titles over-index on this surface; 2,011,304 signups originate here

- Signups and plays on Fire TV, Roku and smart TVs are carried at the individual level exactly as web and mobile are: every session carries its surface, and the account the signup lands on is the same account the later plays attach to, so a Roku signup followed by a phone watch reads as one person on two surfaces, not two people.
- The gap between the two splits is the shape worth holding: connected TV takes 78.3% of the hours but only 38.2% of the signups. Entry leans to the small screen and the browser, where card entry and promo codes are easier, and consumption leans lean-back once the account exists.
- Paramount+ skews harder to the TV screen than a general SVOD audience because of live sports and news, which almost never play on a phone in the home; mobile's 11.6% of hours is weighted to short-form, highlights and out-of-home dayparts.
- The Avid tier is close to fully TV-resident at 93.1% connected TV reach, which reads as the heavy-viewing core being a living-room audience; the mobile-only slice of the total audience skews younger and lighter, and is the part of the base that moves first on a price or packaging change.

How these are counted:
- Window: Nov 16 2025 to Nov 16 2026.
- Base: the Paramount+ (device coverage) audience, measured across 10M US consumers and projected to the US.
- What we count as a view: A view is one person, on any screen, who played a title for at least one second inside the window, counted once however many devices or sessions they used. Autoplayed previews and trailers are not views. Counts are US viewers (persons), not accounts, so they are not comparable to a service's reported subscriber count, to TV ratings, or to platform view counts that tally plays instead of people.
- How Nielsen counts: time viewed, not views. Its streaming charts total the minutes watched on TV screens in the US, without phones or computers, and its TV ratings average the people watching in a typical minute.
- Carriage paths: direct app and site sessions plus channel storefronts (Prime Video Channels, Apple TV Channels, Roku) where the title is attributable.
- Sessions: A session closes after 30 minutes without activity; a backgrounded app is not an open.

On Amazon Prime Video Channels vs direct, premium streaming subscriptions:

People who sign up for a premium streaming service through Amazon cancel 1.7x as often as people who sign up direct: 7.4% monthly churn through Amazon Prime Video Channels against 4.3% direct, same services, same shows, same price in both stores.

We followed 6,214,387 subscriptions to ten premium services sold both ways (HBO Max, Peacock, Paramount+, STARZ, Apple TV+, BET+, MGM+, AMC+, BritBox, Acorn TV) from Nov 1 2025 to Oct 31 2026. 33.4% started in Amazon's store (2,075,611 Amazon starts; 4,138,776 direct).

- Monthly churn: 7.4% through Amazon, 4.3% direct (cancelled in a month over active at the start of the month, averaged across the twelve months, cancel dated to the cancel request).
- Share of new signups still active, from each signup's own day 0: day 30 71.8% Amazon vs 82.3% direct; day 60 55.2% vs 70.1%; day 90 44.7% vs 61.4% (a 16.7 point survival gap at day 90).
- Watched one title and gone within 35 days: 38.2% of Amazon signups vs 24.6% of direct signups.
- Plan mix: 92.3% of Amazon signups sit on month-to-month pricing; direct services move 31.7% of their base onto annual plans and bundles (68.3% month to month).
- Months kept in the first 12: direct 7.9, through Amazon 5.6.
- What a first-year subscriber is worth: direct $101.23 at each service's own list price; through Amazon $70.81 at list, about $49.56 after Amazon's share of the fee. The gap is $30.43 at list, $51.67 after the share.
- Where the cancels go: 41.8% of Amazon cancellers start another streaming service within 30 days, against 29.0% of direct cancellers.
- Winback within 90 days: 18.9% of direct cancellers are back at the same service, against 11.3% through Amazon.
- Price parity: every one of the ten services costs the same on Amazon as direct, ten for ten.
